:-: | :-:

$\redE2$ | $\purpleD{6}$

Now, let's try each rule to see whether it works for all $3$ coordinates.

|| **Multiply $x$ by $4$. Then subtract $1$ from the product to get $y$.** ||
$x$ | $y$ | Matches graph?
:-: | :-: | :-:
$\redE{1}$ | $(4 \times \redE{1})-1=\purpleD{3}$ | Yes
$\redE{2}$ | $(4 \times \redE{2})-1=\purpleD{7}$ | No
$\redE{3}$ | $(4\times \redE{3})-1=\purpleD{11}$ | No

This rule does *not work* for all of the values.

|| **Multiply $x$ by $3$ to get $y$.** ||
$x$ | $y$ | Matches graph?
:-: | :-: | :-:
$\redE{1}$ | $3 \times \redE{1}=\purpleD{3}$ | Yes
$\redE{2}$ | $3 \times \redE{2}=\purpleD{6}$ | Yes
$\redE{3}$ | $3\times \redE{3}=\purpleD{9}$ | Yes

This rule works for all of the values.

This is the completed table.

$x$ | $y$ 
:-: | :-: 
$1$ | $3$
$2$ | $6$
$3$ | $9$

The rule that describes the relationship between $x$ and $y$ is, "Multiply $x$ by $3$ to get $y$."
